params.title: Electrical Math
params.subtitle: Ohm's law, power, frequency error, sine waves, time constants, impedance and power supplies: every calculation worked step by step.

onScreen: Ohm's law, power, frequency error, sine waves, time constants, impedance and power supplies
scenes.narration: This lesson is all about the math on the Element 3 exam. We'll work Ohm's law, power, frequency error, sine waves, time constants, impedance and power supply problems, one step at a time, and land on the exam answer every time. Get a pencil ready. We'll start with the most important formula in electronics: Ohm's law.

params.title: Ohm's law: three forms of one law
steps: Multiply both sides by R: E = I × R
Divide both sides by I: R = E ÷ I
Not I = R ÷ E: that form is upside down
params.answer: E in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms

onScreen: I = R ÷ E is wrong: upside down
scenes.narration: Ohm's law says current equals voltage divided by resistance: I equals E over R. Multiply both sides by R, and you get E equals I times R. Divide both sides by I, and you get R equals E over I. Watch out for I equals R over E. That one is incorrect, because it is upside down. In every form, E is in volts, I is in amperes, and R is in ohms.

Let's use all three forms. 2 amperes flow through a 50 ohm resistor. What's the voltage? E equals I times R: 2 times 50 is 100 volts. Next, a 100 ohm resistor sits across 200 volts. I equals E over R: 200 over 100 is 2 amperes. Last, a resistor carries 3 amperes from 90 volts. R equals E over I: 90 over 3 is 30 ohms. If you multiply instead, you get 270. That's not ohms. That's the power, in watts.

Ohm's law also sizes series resistors. A 50 microamp DC, or direct current, meter must read full scale at 200 volts DC. The series resistor is R equals E over I: 200 volts divided by 50 microamps, which is 4 megohms. Now a relay. Its 500 ohm coil operates on 125 milliamps, and the supply is 110 volts DC. The total resistance needed is 110 volts over 125 milliamps, or 880 ohms. The coil already supplies 500 of those ohms. So the series resistor is 880 minus 500, which is 380 ohms.

Power and resistance give you voltage too. Since P equals E squared over R, E equals the square root of P times R. A 100 watt transmitter feeds a 50 ohm load. The RMS, or root mean square, voltage is the square root of 100 times 50, about 70.7 volts. To get the peak, multiply by 1.414. 70.7 times 1.414 is about 100 volts. Peak-to-peak is twice the peak. So the answer is 200 volts peak-to-peak.

params.title: A resistor's rating sets its limits

scenes.narration: A resistor's wattage rating limits its voltage and current. What's the most DC or RMS voltage across a 20 watt, 2000 ohm resistor? E equals the square root of 20 times 2000. That's the square root of 40,000, which is 200 volts. Next, a 500 ohm, 2 watt resistor in parallel with a 1500 ohm, 1 watt resistor. The first is limited to about 31.6 volts, the second to about 38.7 volts. Parallel resistors share one voltage, so the lower limit governs: 31.6 volts. Finally, current. For a resistor marked 2000 ohms, 200 watts, I equals the square root of P over R. That's the square root of 0.1, about 0.316 amps.

callouts.label: D<sub>1</sub> is reverse biased: it conducts no current
R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> form one series string

onScreen: R1, R2 and R3 in series
scenes.narration: Here's Figure 3B1. A 10 volt battery feeds R1, R2 and R3, with diode D1 connected where R1 meets R2. D1 is reverse biased, so it conducts no current, and you can ignore it. That leaves R1, R2 and R3 as one series string: 300 plus 200 plus 100, or 600 ohms. R1's share of the voltage is its share of the resistance. 10 volts times 300 over 600 gives 5 volts across R1.

params.title: Figure 3B2: the Zener clamps at 3 V

callouts.label: Without the Zener: 12 V × 15k ÷ 25k = 7.2 V across R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub>
7.2 V is more than 3 V, so the 3 V Zener conducts
The Zener clamps that node at 3 V

scenes.narration: Figure 3B2 adds a 3 volt Zener diode. First, ignore the Zener. R2 and R3 total 15 kilohms, and with R1 the whole string is 25 kilohms. So R2 and R3 alone would sit at 12 volts times 15 over 25, which is 7.2 volts. That's more than 3 volts, so the Zener conducts and clamps that node at 3 volts. R1 drops the rest: 12 minus 3, or 9 volts.

onScreen: At 1 ppm, MHz reading = Hz error
scenes.narration: A frequency counter is only as accurate as its time base, and that accuracy is given in ppm, parts per million. The most the real frequency can differ from the reading is the reading times the ppm, divided by 1,000,000. Take a reading of 462,100,000 hertz with a time base of plus or minus 0.1 parts per million. 462,100,000 times 0.1, over 1,000,000, is 46.21 hertz. With a 1.0 part per million time base, it's 462.1 hertz. Here's a shortcut. At 1 part per million, a frequency in megahertz gives the same number in hertz: 462.1 megahertz, 462.1 hertz.

Now a reading of 156,520,000 hertz. With a plus or minus 1.0 part per million time base, the error can be 156,520,000 times 1.0, over 1,000,000. That's 156.52 hertz, just as the shortcut predicts. With a plus or minus 10 parts per million time base, the error is 10 times bigger: 156,520,000 times 10, over 1,000,000, or 1565.20 hertz.

Harmonics are simpler. The second harmonic is twice the fundamental frequency. For a 380 kilohertz signal, the second harmonic is 2 times 380, or 760 kilohertz. For an SSB, or single sideband, transmitter on 4146 kilohertz, the second harmonic is 2 times 4146, or 8292 kilohertz.

params.title: A 5 volt peak sine wave, angle by angle
labels: v = V<sub>peak</sub> × sin θ: positive 0° to 180°, negative 180° to 360°

scenes.narration: The instantaneous value of a sine wave is the peak voltage times the sine of the angle. From 0 to 180 degrees the values are positive. From 180 to 360 degrees they are negative. Take a sine wave with a 5 volt peak. At pi over 3 radians, which is 60 degrees, it's 5 times 0.866, about plus 4.3 volts. At 150 degrees, it's 5 times 0.5, or plus 2.5 volts. At 240 degrees, the sine is minus 0.866, so the wave is at about minus 4.3 volts.

params.title: RMS: the DC voltage that heats the same
params.answer: ≈ 120 volts AC RMS; 170 V is the peak

onScreen: RMS = DC voltage giving the same heating
scenes.narration: What does RMS really mean? The root mean square value of an AC, or alternating current, voltage is equal to the DC voltage that causes the same heating in a given resistor. For a pure sine wave, multiply the peak by 0.707. Say you measure 340 volts peak-to-peak. The peak is half of that: 340 over 2 is 170 volts. Then 0.707 times 170 is about 120 volts AC. Don't stop at 170 volts. That's the peak, not the RMS value.

callouts.label: Waveform A reaches its positive peak…
…at the instant waveform B starts its cycle (the dashed line)
B lags A by 90 degrees: a quarter cycle

scenes.narration: Figure 3B3 shows two sine waves, A and B. Follow the dashed line. Waveform A reaches its positive peak at the very instant waveform B starts its cycle. So B is running a quarter cycle behind A, and a quarter cycle is 90 degrees. Waveform B is lagging waveform A by 90 degrees.

params.title: Power factor
params.answer: PF = cosine of the phase angle

scenes.narration: Power factor, PF, is the cosine of the phase angle between voltage and current. Take an R L, or resistor-inductor, circuit with a 60 degree phase angle. The cosine of 60 degrees is 0.5, so the power factor is 0.5. At 45 degrees, it's about 0.707. At 30 degrees, it's about 0.866. Don't pick 0.577. That's the tangent of 30 degrees, not the cosine. Always use the cosine.

params.title: True power, and halving the resistance
steps: Apparent power = RMS volts × RMS amps
Halve R: P = E² ÷ (R ÷ 2) = 2 × E² ÷ R
params.answer: Half the resistance → double the power

onScreen: True power = apparent power × power factor
RMS volts × RMS amps = apparent power only
scenes.narration: When AC voltage and current are out of phase, find the true power by multiplying the apparent power times the power factor. RMS voltage times RMS current gives you only the apparent power. Now a resistor question. With a constant voltage, power is E squared over R. If you cut the resistance in half, you divide by half as much, so the power dissipation doubles.

params.title: Power relationships to remember
items: 1 horsepower = lifting 550 pounds at the rate of 1 foot per second
Power factor = cos θ: 0.5 at 60°, 0.707 at 45°, 0.866 at 30°
True power = apparent power × power factor
Constant voltage: halve R and the power doubles

scenes.narration: One more number. 746 watts is 1 horsepower. A horsepower is the power needed to lift 550 pounds at the rate of 1 foot per second, and that works out to 746 watts. Let's collect this topic. Power factor is the cosine of the phase angle: 0.5 at 60 degrees, 0.707 at 45 degrees, and 0.866 at 30 degrees. True power is apparent power times power factor. And at constant voltage, half the resistance means double the power.

params.title: RC time constant: the 63.2% point
steps: 1 time constant: charged to 63.2% of the supply
Not 36.8%: that's what's left when discharging
params.answer: τ = RC: the time to charge to 63.2%

scenes.narration: Now time constants. In an RC, or resistor-capacitor, circuit, one time constant is tau equals R times C, in seconds. It's the time required for the capacitor to charge to 63.2 percent of the supply voltage. Don't confuse that with 36.8 percent. That's the voltage left on a discharging capacitor after one time constant, not the charge reached. So remember: one RC time constant, 63.2 percent charged.

params.title: RL time constant: the current builds
steps: 1 time constant: current reaches 63.2% of maximum
The current builds up, not the voltage
The inductor opposes changes in current

onScreen: 1 time constant: current at 63.2% of maximum
scenes.narration: An RL, or resistor-inductor, circuit has a time constant too: tau equals L over R. One time constant is the time required for the current to build up to 63.2 percent of its maximum value. Notice it's the current, not the voltage, that builds up. That's because the inductor opposes changes in current, so the current can only rise gradually.

Here are the four numbers to know. After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches 63.2 percent, and a discharging capacitor is down to 36.8 percent. After two time constants, the capacitor in an RC circuit is charged to 1 minus e to the minus 2, or 86.5 percent of the supply voltage. A discharging capacitor is down to e to the minus 2, or 13.5 percent of its starting voltage.

params.title: Working τ = RC in seconds
steps: Ω × F = seconds; MΩ × µF = seconds too

onScreen: Ohms × farads, or megohms × microfarads, gives seconds
scenes.narration: Let's put numbers in. Tau equals R times C gives seconds when R is in ohms and C is in farads. It also gives seconds with megohms and microfarads. A 100 microfarad capacitor in series with a 470 kilohm resistor: 470,000 ohms times 0.0001 farads is 47 seconds. A 220 microfarad capacitor in parallel with a 1 megohm resistor: 1,000,000 ohms times 0.00022 farads is 220 seconds. In both cases, it's simply R times C.

params.title: Matched pairs: τ stays the same
rows: 100 µF and 470 kΩ, all in series
100 µF and 470 kΩ, all in parallel
220 µF and 1 MΩ, all in parallel
220 µF and 1 MΩ, all in series

scenes.narration: Now two capacitors and two resistors. Take two 100 microfarad capacitors and two 470 kilohm resistors, all in series. The resistance doubles to 940 kilohms, and the capacitance halves to 50 microfarads. 940 kilohms times 50 microfarads is still 47 seconds. All in parallel, it's 235 kilohms times 200 microfarads: 47 seconds again. Two 220 microfarad capacitors and two 1 megohm resistors all in parallel give 0.5 megohms times 440 microfarads, or 220 seconds. All in series, it's 2 megohms times 110 microfarads: 220 seconds.

params.title: Why matched pairs don't change τ
items: All in series: R doubles and C halves
All in parallel: R halves and C doubles
τ equals that of 1 resistor with 1 capacitor: 47 or 220 seconds

onScreen: Same τ as 1 resistor with 1 capacitor
scenes.narration: Here's the shortcut behind that table. When a matched pair of resistors and a matched pair of capacitors are both in series, the resistance doubles and the capacitance halves. When they're both in parallel, the resistance halves and the capacitance doubles. Either way, the doubling and halving cancel. The time constant equals that of one resistor with one capacitor. So the answer stays at 47 seconds, or 220 seconds.

params.title: Rectangular form: an inductor in series
steps: X<sub>L</sub> ≈ 18.8 Ω: inductive, so plus j
R = 20 Ω is the real part

onScreen: Inductive: plus j; capacitive: minus j
scenes.narration: Impedance in rectangular coordinates is written R plus j X. The resistance is the real part. Inductive reactance takes a plus j, and capacitive reactance takes a minus j. Let's try one. A 0.1 microhenry inductor is in series with 20 ohms at 30 megahertz. X sub L equals 2 pi f L: 2 pi times 30 megahertz times 0.1 microhenry is about 18.8 ohms. It's inductive, so it gets a plus j. The 20 ohms is the real part. Rounded, Z equals 20 plus j 19.

params.title: A capacitor in series: minus j
steps: X<sub>C</sub> ≈ 318 Ω: capacitive, so minus j
R = 400 Ω is the real part

scenes.narration: Now a capacitor. A 0.001 microfarad capacitor is in series with 400 ohms at 500 kilohertz. X sub C equals 1 over 2 pi f C. That's 1 over 2 pi times 500 kilohertz times 0.001 microfarads, about 318 ohms. Capacitive reactance takes a minus j. The 400 ohms is the real part. So Z equals 400 minus j 318.

Same method, more networks. Here's the first one again: 20 plus j 19. The same 0.1 microhenry inductor with 30 ohms at 5 megahertz has X sub L of about 3.14 ohms, so Z equals 30 plus j 3. A 10 microhenry inductor with 40 ohms at 500 megahertz has about 31,400 ohms of reactance: 40 plus j 31400. A 1.0 millihenry inductor with 200 ohms at 30 kilohertz gives about 188 ohms: 200 plus j 188. And the capacitor network is 400 minus j 318. Resistance first, then plus j for an inductor, minus j for a capacitor.

params.title: A capacitor in parallel: product over sum

scenes.narration: Parallel networks use product over sum. A 0.01 microfarad capacitor is in parallel with 300 ohms at 50 kilohertz. X sub C works out to about 318 ohms. Multiply 300 by minus j 318, then divide by 300 minus j 318. The result is Z equals 159 minus j 150. The minus j tells you the network is capacitive.

params.title: Polar form: magnitude and angle
items: A polar plot shows a sine-wave voltage's magnitude and phase angle
Phasor length = magnitude; angle from the reference axis = phase
Polar impedance: ohms and an angle, such as 141 ohms, /45 degrees
The slash stands for the angle sign
Inductive angles are positive; capacitive angles are negative

onScreen: Polar plot: magnitude and phase angle
scenes.narration: Polar coordinates describe the same networks another way. A polar plot of a sine-wave voltage shows its magnitude and its phase angle. It's drawn as a phasor: the arrow's length is the magnitude, and its angle from the reference axis is the phase. In polar form, impedance is written as a magnitude in ohms and a phase angle, such as 141 ohms at 45 degrees. On the exam, the slash stands for the angle sign. Inductive angles are positive, and capacitive angles are negative.

params.title: Series: |Z| = √(R² + X²), θ = arctan(X ÷ R)
rows: 600 Ω X<sub>L</sub> − 300 Ω X<sub>C</sub> = 300 Ω, 400 Ω R

onScreen: Series: magnitude √(R² + X²), angle arctan(X ÷ R)
scenes.narration: For R and X in series, the magnitude is the square root of R squared plus X squared, and the angle is the arc tangent of X over R. A 100 ohm reactance inductor with a 100 ohm resistor gives about 141 ohms, at the arc tangent of 1, which is 45 degrees. A 400 ohm reactance capacitor with a 300 ohm resistor gives 500 ohms, at minus the arc tangent of 1.333, about minus 53.1 degrees. Last, a capacitor with 300 ohms of reactance, an inductor with 600 ohms, and a 400 ohm resistor. The reactances cancel to 600 minus 300, or 300 ohms inductive. That gives 500 ohms at about 37 degrees.

params.title: Parallel: an inductor and a resistor
params.formula: |Z| = R × X ÷ √(R² + X²), θ = arctan(R ÷ X)

scenes.narration: Parallel networks use a different formula. The magnitude is R times X, over the square root of R squared plus X squared. The angle is the arc tangent of R over X. A 400 ohm reactance inductor is in parallel with a 300 ohm resistor. The magnitude is 300 times 400, divided by the square root of 300 squared plus 400 squared. That's 300 times 400 over 500, or 240 ohms. The angle is the arc tangent of 0.75, about 36.9 degrees, positive because it's inductive. Z equals 240 ohms at 36.9 degrees.

params.title: Parallel: a capacitor and a resistor

scenes.narration: One more. A 100 picofarad capacitor is in parallel with a 4000 ohm resistor at 500 kilohertz. X sub C is about 3183 ohms. The square root of 4000 squared plus 3183 squared is about 5112. So the magnitude is 4000 times 3183 over 5112, about 2490 ohms. The angle is minus the arc tangent of 1.257, about minus 51.5 degrees. It's negative because the network is capacitive. Z equals 2490 ohms at minus 51.5 degrees.

params.title: Impedance magnitude: don't just add
steps: Not 6 + 17: R and X<sub>L</sub> are 90° apart

scenes.narration: A series circuit has 6 ohms of resistance, 17 ohms of inductive reactance, and no capacitive reactance. What's the magnitude of its impedance? Use the square root of R squared plus X sub L squared. That's the square root of 6 squared plus 17 squared, which is the square root of 325. That's about 18 ohms. Don't just add 6 and 17. That ignores the 90 degree phase difference between resistance and reactance.

params.title: Biasing a Zener at its midpoint

blocks.label: 10 V Zener, 20 V supply
blocks.note: I min. 5 mA, I max. 95 mA

onScreen: 10 V Zener: 5 to 95 mA, on a 20 V supply
scenes.narration: Now a Zener diode bias problem. A 10 volt Zener has a minimum current of 5 milliamps and a maximum of 95 milliamps. We want to bias it at its midpoint from a 20 volt supply. The midpoint current is 5 plus 95, over 2, which is 50 milliamps. The resistor drops the difference between the supply and the Zener: 20 minus 10, or 10 volts. So R equals 10 volts over 50 milliamps, which is 200 ohms.

params.title: Percentage voltage regulation
steps: Based on full load: E<sub>NL</sub> = E<sub>FL</sub> × (1 + 0.25)

scenes.narration: Power supply regulation compares the no-load voltage with the full-load voltage. Percentage regulation is the no-load voltage minus the full-load voltage, divided by the full-load voltage, times 100 percent. A supply gives 12 volts with no load and 10 volts at full load. 12 minus 10, over 10, times 100 percent, is 20 percent. Because regulation is based on the full-load voltage, you can work backward. A 200 volt full-load voltage with 25 percent regulation gives a no-load voltage of 200 times 1.25, or 250 volts.

params.title: Turns ratio and conductance
steps: 50 to 1 is the impedance ratio, not the turns ratio
Conductance: R = 12 V ÷ 6 A = 2 Ω, G = 1 ÷ R

scenes.narration: A transformer's impedance ratio is the square of its turns ratio. So to match 500 ohms to 10 ohms, the turns ratio is the square root of 500 over 10. That's the square root of 50, about 7.1, a 7.1 to 1 turns ratio. 50 to 1 is the impedance ratio, not the turns ratio. Last, conductance, G, is the reciprocal of resistance. 6 amperes flow at 12 volts DC, so R is 2 ohms. G equals 1 over 2, or 0.50 siemens, also called mhos. That's the same as I over E: 6 over 12.
